svg.text: Labels, audit and patient splits in CBIS-DDSM — a visual lesson
Step 2 of the pipeline, explained on our own data. Every picture is a real case from data/raw; every number was measured on data/interim/manifest.csv on 2026-09-16.
What you will be able to do after this sheet
1. Read a CBIS-DDSM label: which file is the network's input, which is its target, and how a CSV row points to the pixels.
2. Explain why the masks of one image are fused before training, using the arithmetic of the loss.
3. Follow the audit: what each check catches, and why the checks run in that order.
4. Build a validation set that does not leak: group by patient, stratify by pathology.
How to read it
Four lessons, top to bottom. Each one opens with the question it answers, explains
the mechanism in words (left), shows it on real images (right), then closes with
three boxes:
Key idea — what to remember. Watch out — the classic mistake. In our data — the
measured numbers.
Glossary and self-check questions are at the bottom.
Lesson 1 — What exactly is a label?
When we say “the label of a lesion”, what is stored, and where?
BUILT
src/cbis_ddsm/data/manifest.py · scripts/build_manifest.py
A mammogram is a grayscale picture of X-rays passing through the breast. Dense
tissue and masses absorb more X-rays, so they look brighter. Each breast is
usually imaged twice: CC (cranio-caudal, from above) and MLO (medio-lateral
oblique, from the side, at an angle).
The label is an image. For every lesion a radiologist drew its outline. CBIS-
DDSM does not store that outline as a list of coordinates: it stores it as a
second image, the ROI mask ②, with exactly the same width and height as the
mammogram ①. In the mask a pixel is white (255) inside the outline and black
(0) outside.
Aligned, pixel for pixel. Because the two images line up pixel for pixel, the
mask answers one yes/no question for every pixel of the mammogram: is this
pixel part of the lesion? ③ shows it by drawing the mask's border on the
mammogram. Training a segmentation network means teaching it to give that
answer by itself, from the mammogram alone.
The cropped image ④ is a close-up cut out of the mammogram around the lesion.
It helps a human look at the lesion; our network uses it neither as input nor
as target.
How a CSV row leads to the pixels
a
mass_case_description_train_set.csv
One row per lesion: P_00001, LEFT, CC, abnormality 1, MALIGNANT, … and three file
references ending in .dcm (the original DICOM format).
b
dicom_info.csv
The .dcm files are not in the Kaggle download. This table translates each .dcm
reference into the path of its .jpg (10 237 entries).
c
jpeg/<series id>/1-250.jpg
The actual pixels. 6 774 folders, 8-bit JPEGs converted from 16-bit DICOM, so a
little detail was lost.
d
data/interim/manifest.csv
manifest.py writes one clean row per lesion: patient, side, view, abnormality,
pathology, density, assessment + the 3 jpg paths.
P_00001 · left breast · CC view · abnormality 1 · malignant · spiculated margins
① Full mammogram 4808×3024
the network's INPUT. Red box:
where the lesion is.
② ROI mask 4808×3024
the TARGET. Same size as ①. White
= lesion (0.83 % of the pixels).
③ Overlay (zoom)

Key idea
A label is an image, not a description. Pixel (x, y) of
the mask is the answer for pixel (x, y) of the mammogram.
Watch out
The crop and the mask of a lesion often sit in the same
folder, and their CSV columns are sometimes swapped.
manifest.py tells them apart by content. JPEG also turns
255 into values like 249: test “≥ 245”, never “= 255”.
In our data
3 567 lesion rows, 1 696 of them masses. Full mammograms
are about 5 200 × 3 000 pixels. In P_00001 the lesion
covers 0.83 % of the pixels: over 99 % of a mammogram is
background.
In this lesson
• the three files of a lesion
• input vs target
• from a CSV row to the pixels
Lesson 2 — Why fuse the masks of one image?
One image can hold several lesions, each with its own mask. Which target should the network see?
PLANNED — NOT CODED YET
next: fusion in the dataset preparation
Rows are lesions, training examples are images. The manifest has one row per
lesion, but the network learns from images — more precisely from patches, small
squares cut out of an image at full resolution. When an image holds three
lesions, the dataset gives three mask files, each white only on its own lesion.
Fusion builds one target per image: stack the masks and keep, for every pixel,
the largest value. The pixel is lesion if at least one radiologist outline
covers it. No search over coordinates is needed — the masks are already arrays
of the same size, so it is one pixel-by-pixel operation.
M(x, y) = max( m1(x, y), m2(x, y), m3(x, y) )
What goes wrong without it. Suppose we cut a patch for lesion 2 and give it
only mask m2 as target. Lesion 1 is visible in the patch but labelled 0 (red
area on the right). The loss now punishes the network for seeing a real mass:
Worked example — the loss on that pixel
BCE (binary cross-entropy) charges every pixel labelled 0 a cost of −log(1 −
p), where p is the network's predicted probability of “lesion”.
Pixel on lesion 1, network answers p = 0.9 → cost −log(0.1) = 2.30
Same pixel, network answers p = 0.1 → cost −log(0.9) = 0.11
The gradient pushes p down: the network is trained to ignore a real mass. Dice
= 2 × overlap ÷ (predicted area + true area): predicting lesion 1 grows the
predicted area but not the overlap, so Dice drops too.
Keep both. With M as target, lesion 1 is labelled 1 and a correct prediction is
rewarded. We still keep m1, m2, m3 apart: evaluation counts which lesions were
found or missed, and the fused mask can no longer tell them apart.

Key idea
Train on one fused mask per image; evaluate with the per-
lesion masks.
Watch out
Fuse only masks of the same image (same patient, side and
view). CC and MLO are two different projections: their
pixels do not correspond. And if one lesion of a multi-
lesion image is excluded, the fused mask is incomplete —
exclude the whole image.
In our data
71 of the 1 592 mass images hold 2 or more lesions (175
lesions, about 10 %). 8 of them mix benign and malignant
lesions. None of them contains one of the 78 lesions
excluded by the audit.
In this lesson
• rows vs training examples
• the max rule
• what the loss does to an
incomplete target
Lesson 3 — The audit: which rows can we trust?
Before training, how do we find broken rows — and record the ones we drop?
BUILT · RUN ON THE 1 696 MASSES
src/cbis_ddsm/data/audit.py · scripts/audit_data.py
First failure wins. Every lesion row goes through five checks, in a fixed order
(right). The first check that fails gives the row its exclusion reason and the
row stops there. So each excluded row has exactly one reason, and the counts
add up: 1 696 in = 1 618 kept + 78 excluded.
Why this order. Fundamental checks come first: a missing file makes every later
check impossible. Size comes before content, because the pixel values of a mask
that does not line up with its image mean nothing. Binarity comes before
emptiness: a mask full of grey noise is corrupted, and calling it “empty” would
hide the real problem.
Case study. The only failure on our masses is dimension_mismatch, 78 rows. All
78 masks are smaller than their mammogram by the same factor, 0.870, on both
axes: the mask was saved at a lower resolution. Read as is, its white area sits
away from the lesion (right, red).
The cropped image is an exact cut-out of the mammogram, so we can find where it
came from (match score ≈ 1.00) and use that as the lesion's true position.
Distance from there to the centre of the mask:
Mask used
median distance
verdict
normal rows (30 sampled)
7 px
reference
mismatched mask, read as is
404 px
wrong place
mismatched mask, stretched ×1/0.87
40 px
75 of 78 under 150 px
So: Stretching brings the contour back onto the lesion, but less precisely than
a normal row (40 px vs 7 px). The decision is still open: keep excluding
(current), or stretch and verify — and document the choice.
The five checks, in order
1 696 mass rows enter
missing_path
a file listed in the manifest is not on disk
0 out
duplicate_lesion
two rows share patient, side, view and
abnormality number
0 out
dimension_mismatch
mask and mammogram differ in size: pixels no
longer line up
78 out
non_binary_mask
the mask holds grey values: corrupted, or not
a mask
0 out
empty_mask
no white pixel: no lesion to learn from
0 out
1 618 rows kept → exclusions.csv keeps the 78
P_00145 · left CC · benign
mask read as is
red: off target
mask stretched

Key idea
An exclusion is a traced decision, not a silent deletion:
every dropped row keeps one reason in exclusions.csv, so
anyone can recount and challenge it.
Watch out
These counts are lesion rows. Rows (1 696), images (1
592), patients (892) and files are four different numbers
— never quote one in place of another.
In our data
Masses: 1 696 rows → 78 dimension_mismatch → 1 618 kept
(1 253 train, 365 test). Before the audit, building the
manifest dropped a single row, a calcification whose file
reference could not be found.
In this lesson
• five checks, one reason per
row
• why the order matters
• the 78 undersized masks
Lesson 4 — Splitting by patient, and stratifying
How do we build a validation set that tells the truth about new patients?
PLANNED — NOT CODED YET
next: src/cbis_ddsm/data/splits.py · scripts/make_splits.py · tests/test_splits.py
Three partitions, three jobs. Train: the network learns its weights on it.
Validation: we use it to choose — when to stop, which threshold, which model.
Test: judged once, at the very end. Every choice made while looking at a
partition makes its score a little optimistic; that is why the test stays
sealed until the end.
Leakage. CBIS-DDSM ships an official train/test split with no shared patient
(we checked). Validation must be cut out of train, and that is where leakage
appears. If rows are assigned at random, the CC view of a mass can land in
train and the MLO view of the same mass in validation. The network has then
already seen that mass and that breast: the validation score measures memory,
not generalisation.
Grouping. Assign patients, not rows: all the rows of a patient go to the same
partition. In set notation: train patients ∩ validation patients = ∅ (no
patient in both).
Stratification. With about 690 patients, a random cut could put many more
malignant cases in validation than in train, and the scores would not be
comparable. Stratifying keeps the malignant share similar everywhere. Because
we split patients, each patient needs one label: “has at least one malignant
mass” or not.
StratifiedGroupKFold (from scikit-learn) does both at once: it deals patients
into 5 folds of similar size and similar malignant share. Fold 0 becomes
validation, folds 1–4 are train. Rotating the validation fold later gives
cross-validation.

Output: data/splits/split_v1.json + tests/test_splits.py
The file stores the seed, a fingerprint of the manifest and the patient IDs of every fold. Every
experiment reads this same file, so all models are compared on the same patients.
Tests: no patient in both train and validation · no train or validation patient in test · every kept
row assigned exactly once · same seed ⇒ identical file.
Key idea
Split patients, not rows — the patient is the unit we
want the model to work on. Stratify on a label defined
per patient.
Watch out
Stratifying rows while grouping patients is
contradictory: define the patient label first. And 13 of
our mass-train patients have calcifications in the
official test — harmless now, a leak on the day
calcifications are added.
In our data
691 train / 201 test patients, 0 in common. 509 of the
722 train breasts with a mass are imaged in both CC and
MLO, so a row-level split would leak for most patients.
Patient label: 346 with a malignant mass, 345 without; 13
patients have both kinds.

Summary, glossary and self-check
The whole step in four sentences
1. A label is an image aligned with the mammogram: one yes/no answer per pixel.
2. The network trains on one fused target per image; per-lesion masks are kept for evaluation.
3. Five checks run in order and every dropped row keeps exactly one traced reason.
4. Validation is cut by patient, stratified on a per-patient label, and the test stays sealed.
Check yourself — answer before moving on
Q1. A mask pixel reads 249. Lesion or background? Why is the test not “= 255”?
Q2. Nothing is duplicated, yet a split by image instead of by patient inflates validation Dice. Why?
Q3. A patch cut for lesion 2 of P_00106 uses mask m2 only. What does BCE teach the network about lesion
Q4. Why is non_binary_mask checked before empty_mask?
Q5. A patient has one benign and one malignant mass. Which stratification label does this patient get,
and what would change with the opposite rule?
Glossary
ROI mask
Image the size of the mammogram; white = inside the radiologist's outline.
Patch
Small square cut from an image at full resolution; the same square is cut from the mask.
CC / MLO
The two standard views of a breast: from above / from the side at an angle.
BCE
Binary cross-entropy: per-pixel penalty, large when a confident prediction is wrong.
Dice
2 × overlap ÷ (predicted area + true area); 1 = perfect, 0 = no overlap.
Leakage
Information from validation or test reaching training, which inflates scores.
Grouping
Keeping all rows of one patient in the same partition.
Stratification
Keeping the share of a label (here malignant) similar across partitions.
Fold
One of k equal parts of the data; each takes a turn as validation.
Assessment
BI-RADS score 0–5 given by the radiologist; recorded, not used as input.
Density
Breast density 1–4; dense breasts hide lesions. Used to stratify results.
Subtlety
0–5, how hard the lesion is to see. In the CSVs, not yet in the manifest.
Legend
Key idea — to remember
Watch out — common mistake or excluded rows
In our data — measured facts
Worked example
BUILT — code exists and was run
PLANNED — not coded yet
Thumbnails are shrunk for display only; training never shrinks the whole mammogram. Sources: data/raw (Kaggle CBIS-DDSM JPEG mirror), data/interim/manifest.csv, docs/PROTOCOLE.md.
